summary: Round 5, verify. Re-ran a 51-mutant matrix over Checkpoint.java against :format:test with --rerun-tasks: 45/51 killed (88.2%), and every one of the six survivors is an entry in baselines/mutants.txt. Zero unargued survivors. The carried MAJOR tr-10 is closed by measurement: with each < 0 half deleted individually, s1-streamCountNEGhalf, c1-podCountNEGhalf, l1-podLenNEGhalf and p1-partitionNEGhalf are all KILLED. The hand-built objects are stronger than the prescription I gave in round 4, not merely different: each ends after the field under test so the mutant ACCEPTS rather than refusing with a different message, which is a kill by decode-returned-normally and not only by message text. Carried majors tr-1, tr-2 and tr-7 also measured killed. One minor.

findings.finding: The requireNonNull equivalence argument says 'new LinkedHashMap<>(null) raises NullPointerException either way'. Measured with both parameter checks deleted, that holds for new Checkpoint(1, null, Map.of()) and new Checkpoint(1, Map.of(), null) -- both NPE 'Cannot invoke java.util.Map.size() because m is null'. It does NOT hold for new Checkpoint(-1, null, Map.of()): with the checks present that is NPE, without them the sequence < 0 guard fires first and it is IllegalArgumentException. The exception TYPE changes, which is more than the message the entry claims. The conclusion still stands -- a caller error is refused with an unchecked exception either way and no caller can depend on which -- so this is a precision defect in the prose, not a wrong licence. Not worth fixing in a sixth round; the file's own header is the right place for it if it is ever touched again.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone reads the entry as measured fact, deletes both parameter checks, and a caller that passes a negative sequence together with a null map now gets IllegalArgumentException where the entry promised NullPointerException. Nothing downstream branches on that, so no defect follows -- but the file opens by saying a wrong equivalence argument is worse than an unargued survivor, and this one is imprecise in the same direction as the two it just removed.
findings.mutation_that_survives: Objects.requireNonNull(streams, "streams") and Objects.requireNonNull(pods, "pods") deleted -- r6/r7, both measured SURVIVED, both argued.

resolved.evidence: Each < 0 disjunct deleted individually against :format:test --rerun-tasks: streamCount KILLED, podCount KILLED, podLen KILLED, partitionId KILLED. Also measured: the whole-guard and > limit halves of all three counts (s2/s3, c2/c3, l2/l3, p2/p3) are KILLED. The crafted objects at CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest.java:263-285 end exactly after the field under test, so without its guard each object DECODES SUCCESSFULLY -- a checkpoint with no streams, a checkpoint with no pods, and a pod 'p' with flushSeq 7 -- rather than being refused by the trailing-bytes check. That is a stronger detector than the three hasMessageContaining assertions I prescribed in round 4, because it does not depend on message text to distinguish two refusals.
The false entry arguing streamCount < 0 and podLen < 0 as equivalent is REMOVED from baselines/mutants.txt, and both halves are now killed by test (s1, l1).
The claim that podCount < 0 was killed by a splice-based test is gone; c1-podCountNEGhalf is now genuinely KILLED by an object that ends after the pod count.
The splice at CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest.java:250-253 that left six trailing bytes is replaced by raw()-built objects with no trailing bytes; measured, the mutant that survived it is now killed.
The line arguing the negative counts as zero-iteration-then-trailing-bytes is removed; the measurement it contradicted (accept, not refuse) is what the new objects demonstrate.

Not in scope for this round but cheap to check with the harness already built. Dropping the partitionId leg of RunKey.compareTo fails 5 of 198 :format tests; replacing Collections.sort(keys) with a sort by indexId alone fails 2. The idx(3)/partition 9 and idx(3)/partition 4 pair in CheckpointTest.fixture() is what pins the tiebreak.
h1-shortHeaderBound (bytes.length < 8 -> < 7), h2-magicCheckDeleted and h3-versionCheckDeleted are all KILLED, as are h4 (MAGIC constant changed) and h5 (VERSION constant changed).
d2-repeatPodGuard KILLED by aREPEATEDPodIsRefusedToo; d1-repeatStreamGuard KILLED.

t2-iaeWrapRemoved (rethrow the IllegalArgumentException instead of wrapping it) is KILLED, so the wrap itself is pinned by aTORNObjectIsAnIOExceptionRatherThanAnUncheckedOne. The comment's ENUMERATION of routes remains untested, but it is now checkable rather than a count: verified by reading that sequence, both offsets, podId (isBlank) and flushSeq each feed a validating record, and that partitionId cannot -- RunKey's only other check is partitionId < 0, which the decoder's [0, Integer.MAX_VALUE] bound preempts. Removing the thrice-wrong count is the right remedy, not an evasion: nothing pinned the number so every value survived every mutation, whereas the enumeration can be falsified by reading. Carried, unchanged in severity, from the round that raised it.
WIDE_ONE's duplicated javadoc is gone and WIDE_NEGATIVE carries its own; :format:compileJava and :format:compileTestJava with --rerun-tasks emit no dangling-doc warning.
